We validate this approach in both controlled and in-thewild settings. In Multi-PIE, we design a controlled experiment to show that fairness gaps can change significantly without modifying the model or its predictions, solely due to differences in visual condition distributions. We then analyze three in-the-wild FER datasets: Aff-Wild2, RAF-DB and AffectNet+. Our results show that the impact of visual confounders is dataset-dependent. It is more pronounced in Aff-Wild2, especially for head pose, and less marked in AffectNet+ and RAF-DB, where visual factor distributions per demographic subgroup are naturally more aligned.  
Overall, our results show that demographic bias estimation in FER can be skewed by unequal visual conditions, although the magnitude of this effect varies across datasets and confounding factors. Our standardized evaluation provides a simple, model-agnostic way to disentangle intrinsic  
model bias from dataset composition, leading to more reliable fairness measurements.  
Our main contributions are as follows:  
- We identify visual factors, such as head pose and illumination, as critical confounders in fairness evaluation for FER.

chunks.paper: Deconfounding demographic bias estimation in facial expression recognition
chunks.text: _Ensuring demographic fairness has become a critical requirement for face processing technologies, and particularly for Facial Expression Recognition (FER). While it is well-established in the literature that visual confounders like head pose strongly affect the recognition performance of FER algorithms, their impact on the estimation of fairness has been overlooked. If demographic groups are observed under unequal visual conditions, usual performance comparisons can be heavily confounded. In this work, we analyze the impact of prominent visual confounders such as head pose and illumination on the estimation of gender bias. Through a controlled study on the Multi-PIE dataset, we show that unequal distributions of just one confounding factor can significantly distort the estimation of demographic bias. To address this, we propose a simple confounder-standardized evaluation protocol and test it on three in-the-wild datasets: Aff-Wild2, RAF-DB and AffectNet+. Our results reveal that the confounding effect is dataset-dependent. For example, in Aff-Wild2, the empirical fairness gap under head pose confounding increases from 4.23% to 6.25% once standardized. Ultimately, our findings

However, the standardized fairness gap in the biased subset is 4.29%, which remains much closer to the empirical fairness gap observed under the balanced condition.  
Since both evaluation conditions are drawn from the same balanced test pool and use the same model, these differences can only be attributed to the head pose composition of the evaluation subset. Overall, this controlled experiment shows that head pose acts as a visual confounder in fairness evaluation. More importantly, it shows that when the evaluation data cannot be fully balanced, the proposed standardized metric can recover a fairness estimate that remains close to the one obtained under balanced conditions, and therefore better reflects the underlying subgroup disparity.

We evaluate the proposed factor-standardized fairness protocol in both controlled and in-the-wild settings. For the controlled study, we use Multi-PIE [7], which provides a suitable benchmark to analyze the effect of head pose under structured acquisition conditions. This controlled environment allows us to isolate the impact of head pose by artificially varying its distribution across demographic groups in the test set. By doing so, we can demonstrate how the measured fairness gap changes due to dataset composition.  
For the in-the-wild analysis, we use Aff-Wild2 [13–16], AffectNet+ [6], and RAF-DB [17]. These datasets exhibit different degrees of variability in head pose and illumination, making them suitable for studying whether visual confounders can influence fairness evaluation in realistic conditions.

chunks.section: 2. Related Work > 2.3. Data Composition and Subgroup Bias
chunks.text:
When demographic subgroups are unevenly distributed across challenging ‘in-the-wild’ conditions ( _e.g_ ., extreme yaw or low illumination), the resulting performance gap is not a pure measure of demographic bias, but a reflection of subgroup imbalance in visual factors. In face analysis, previous work [1, 28] has highlighted that balancing a dataset only at the demographic level may not be sufficient if other important variables remain unbalanced. This perspective is especially relevant for fairness evaluation, since an empirical demographic gap may reflect both intrinsic model behavior and differences in the visual conditions under which each subgroup is evaluated.  
While previous studies focus on identifying performance gaps [19, 29] or proposing algorithmic mitigation [3, 22], our work focuses on the evaluation process itself. Specifically, we address a critical flaw in demographic bias estimation: the compositional confounding that occurs when visual factors and demographic labels are correlated. chunks.paper: Deconfounding demographic bias estimation in facial expression recognition
chunks.text: A primary limitation of our proposal is its heavy reliance on annotated confounding factors and sufficient sample density. Because our method requires evaluating performance within specific visual bins, increasing the number of confounders simultaneously ( _e.g_ ., pose, illumination, and resolution) exponentially increases the amount of data required to maintain stable estimates. In small or highly imbalanced datasets, this can lead to insufficient support for certain demographic-by-confounder combinations. Nevertheless, this extensive data requirement is an unavoidable necessity for rigorous fairness evaluation; without it, any measured bias remains inherently entangled with dataset composition. This highlights a critical need for the community to collect and annotate large-scale datasets with both demographic and environmental diversity in mind.

chunks.paper: Learning to Detect and Describe a Wireframe
chunks.text:
We presented the first unified neural network architecture that jointly detects and describes image wireframes by seamlessly integrating keypoint and line segment extraction into a single, efficient framework. This integration offers both advantages and challenges in combining multiple tasks into a single model. By leveraging a novel multitask distillation strategy, we transfer knowledge from state-of-the-art teacher models into a compact and shared encoder-decoder network. Our approach not only maintains competitive accuracy in terms of keypoint repeatability and matching quality, but also substantially reduces inference time and parameter count. The model’s ability to perform both tasks in parallel makes it well-suited for real-time applications, such as SLAM and 12 I. Ferre et al. (a) Keypoints (b) Keypoints (c) Lines (d) Lines

chunks.paper: Learning to Detect and Describe a Wireframe
chunks.text:
We train the model using a multitask distillation framework that integrates knowledge from two independent teacher networks, one for lines and one for keypoints. Instead of relying solely on final outputs, the student learns from intermediate feature representations, enabling more efficient knowledge transfer. The training minimizes the discrepancy between the student and teacher feature maps via a weighted _L_ 2 loss, balancing contributions from each task and promoting both robustness and computational efficiency.  
We evaluate our method by comparing its performance to the teacher models and state-of-the-art methods on the HPatches and Wireframe datasets. We assess the repeatability of our detections and the quality of our matches. The proposed model is also analyzed in terms of inference speed and parameter efficiency, highlighting improvements over the individual teacher networks and demonstrating the benefits of the multitask distillation approach.  
In summary, our main contributions are:  
- We propose the first model that jointly detects and describes image wireframes.

chunks.paper: Learning to Detect and Describe a Wireframe
chunks.text:
We introduce a unified multitask distillation framework for simultaneous keypoint and line segment detection and description. Our method distills from two teachers, HAWP [24] for line detection, and DISK [21] for keypoint detection, both open-source models with permissive license. We train a compact student model, reducing redundancy, and ensuring consistent feature representations. This makes it ideal for real-time, high-accuracy applications such as robotics, augmented reality, and 3D reconstruction.  
The approach uses a shared encoder-decoder architecture. We initialize the encoder with DISK’s pre-trained weights. Next, each decoder specializes in one task. Task-specific heads refine these outputs into the final predictions, achieving performance on par with the teacher models while significantly reducing computational complexity. HAWP provides expertise in detecting line segments and their connections as graphs, while DISK excels at identifying keypoints and generating robust descriptors. Through knowledge distillation, the student model inherits the strengths of both teachers, ensuring a seamless and unified detection process.

chunks.paper: Learning to Detect and Describe a Wireframe
chunks.text:
Classical corner [6,18,16,17], blob [12,2], and line detectors [4,22,19] directly use image intensities or their gradients to detect distinctive features. Modern approaches leverage deep learning to improve robustness and semantic awareness.  
SuperPoint [3] uses a single encoder to detect corners and generate descriptors, training on synthetic data and refining on real images via homographic adaptation. DISK [21] trains a U-Net end-to-end with reinforcement learning,  
4 I. Ferre et al.  
rewarding keypoints that improve matching. ALIKED [27] pairs an encoder with a lightweight decoder and uses deformable convolutions along with sub-pixel keypoint supervision (via a Neural Reprojection Error) to compensate for reduced depth. Deformable convolutions run fast with a custom CUDA implementation but are hard to port.  
In the domain of line segments, local methods such as LSD [22] or ELSED [19] offer fast and accurate alternatives to the classical Hough Transform [4]. However, they ignore scene semantics, suffer from viewpoint inconsistencies, and are sensitive to lighting variations.

chunks.paper: Learning to Detect and Describe a Wireframe
chunks.text: The multitask model is implemented using PyTorch Lightning and trained for 35 epochs until convergence, using a combined dataset of COCO [10] and Wireframe (train split) [8], containing approximately 13,000 examples per epoch. We used Adam optimizer with an initial learning rate of 1 _×_ 10<sup>_−_4</sup> , which was reduced whenever the validation loss plateaued. The model took around 12 hours to train on an NVIDIA A100 GPU.
